title: The battle for the Senate could go so many different ways | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Imagine when the dust settles on the 2026 midterm elections that Democrats haven’t gained a single Senate seat and are stuck at 47.

Now imagine it’s a week after the election, and Democrats have won 55 seats — or even as many 57 — giving them the second-largest Senate majority for either party since 1981.

The distance between those two outcomes isn’t nearly as large as you might think.

With just five days left in the 2026 election, there is a huge margin of error in the battle for the Senate — with many races showing no clear leader in the polls.

More than a dozen seats have polled mostly within the margin of error (six seats) or just outside of it (five seats), or the races appear competitive but there’s not high-quality polling (two others).

Also looming large is the fact that Democrats are mostly chasing states that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024 — and where it’s feasible that large numbers of conservative voters come home to their side at the very end of the election.

Let’s break it down.

RecentNew York Times/SienaandCNN pollshave filled out the picture in many key Senate races. And several races that are likely to determine the majority are well within the margin of error.

The CNN poll inMichiganshows Democrat Abdul El-Sayed up by 7 points, but 6 of the last 8 quality polls there have shown no clear leader.

Likewise, the CNN poll inTexasshows Democrat James Talarico ahead by 6 points, but 6 of the last 9 quality polls have shown no clear leader.

The CNN poll inKansasis now the second of two quality polls to show no clear leader.

The last five quality polls in Iowa have shown no clear leader.

Thefirst quality poll in South Carolinathis week was a dead heat, at 48%-48%.

And CNN’s poll inMainemakes it six quality polls in a row — and 11 of the past 12 — where there has been no clear leader.

Even if we assume only those races are in-play — and the rest of the races go as expected — the possible outcomes range between Democrats winning 49 seats and winning 55 seats.

(That’s a one-third chance of Democrats remaining in the minority; Democrats winning 50 seats would keep Republicans in control, by virtue of Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote.)

Beyond those six races:

If Democrats were able to win all the margin-of-error races; plus North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska, where the polls are more in their favor; and add Florida and Mississippi, they’d be up to 57 seats. The GOP losing Nebraska would make the Democratic majority 57-42, if Osborn didn’t caucus with either party.

Only once since 1981 has one side or the other controlled more of the Senate than that. That was after the 2008 election, when Democrats had 59 seats (and later won a special election to get to 60 seats).

But it’s also possible Democrats could have a pretty good election, notching one of the biggest popular-vote wins in recent decades, and still come up short of a Senate majority. That could happen if they lose one or both of Maine and Michigan, or if they don’t win enough of the double-digit Trump states they’ve been chasing.

Even if the popular-vote margin from the 2024 presidential race moved uniformly toward Democrats by 10 points in every state, that only gets them to 49 Senate seats.

And it’s worth noting that in CNN’s polls of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, at least 1 in 8 likely voters say they could still change their minds about whom to support. In Texas and Kansas, at least 6 in 10 of those uncommitted likely voters are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, suggesting there is room for political gravity to work in the GOP’s favor as voters settle on their decisions.

In other words, buckle up. The battle for the Senate could go so many different ways, with massive implications for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
